---
title: "7.4 Assumptions"
order: 4
---

Five assumptions carry the output. For each: what it is, the evidence, and what breaks if it
fails. One holds, three hold only in part or nominally, and the last is the one every chapter
rests on.

## The label looks forward {#ews-the-label-looks-forward}

**The assumption.** `{{< var ews.target >}}` is an outcome *after* the behaviour the features
summarise: the model sees an account's history up to now and predicts what happens next. That
is what an early-warning model is for, and what its name says.

**The evidence.** In the generator the label is not later than the features. It is drawn
once, from a logit of the account's true PD, its utilisation over the last three months of the
panel, the change in its utilisation from the first month to the last, and its leverage
([7.2](data.qmd#ews-label)) — quantities measured over the same months the features are built
from. Several features are close transforms of the label's drivers: `util_recent` and
`utilization_onbook` are the recent utilisation, and `util_drift` measures the same rise. The
generator has no calendar beyond the panel, so no out-of-time sample exists either; as for
the scorecard, train and held-out are random splits of one cohort (D4 finding 1).

The assumption **holds only nominally**. The model is a contemporaneous classifier of a
label drawn from the panel's own months, not a forecast across a gap in time.

**What breaks if it fails.** On a real book the label would be observed over a window after
the features, the behaviour driving it would partly happen in that gap, and some of
what the features show now would no longer be true then. Performance across a real forecast
horizon is untested here and would plausibly be lower than the held-out figures in
[7.5](performance.qmd); that is not measured. The monitoring plan measures capture on each new
cohort with matured outcomes, which is the first out-of-time test this model will get
([7.8](monitoring.qmd)).

## The tiers are a fixed review workload {#ews-tiers-as-a-fixed-mix}

**The assumption.** The cutoffs `t_high` and `t_med` are not risk limits stated as
probabilities. They are the {{< var ews.q_high >}} and {{< var ews.q_med >}} quantiles of
the model's probability, re-taken on every retrain ([7.3](methodology.qmd#ews-tiers)). What
the bank fixes is the **review workload** — the share of the book in each tier — and the
probability that separates the tiers follows from the model. The assumption is that the mix
the cutoffs are set to give over the book is the mix they will give on the accounts that get
reviewed.

**The evidence.** The quantiles are taken over all {{< var ews.n_book >}} booked accounts,
of which {{< var ews.n_train >}} are the model's training rows. On those rows the model is
almost perfect (training AUC {{< var ews.train.auc >}}), so their probabilities spread to the
extremes; the upper quantile is set largely by training rows the model has memorised. On the
held-out accounts the mix is very different:

| Tier | Share by construction, the whole book | Share on the held-out accounts |
|---|---|---|
| High | {{< var ews.tier.High.share >}} | {{< var ews.tier_ho.High.share >}} |
| Medium | {{< var ews.tier.Medium.share >}} | {{< var ews.tier_ho.Medium.share >}} |
| Low | {{< var ews.tier.Low.share >}} | {{< var ews.tier_ho.Low.share >}} |

The population stability index between the two mixes is {{< var ews.tier_ho.psi_vs_book >}}:
above the {{< var monitoring.psi_watch >}} the monitoring plan reads as a shift worth watching.
A new account is out-of-sample, so the held-out row is the better guide to the mix the tiers
will give on new business. The assumption **holds in part**: the cutoffs do what the code
says, but not on the accounts the model has not seen — finding 1 ([7.7](limitations.qmd)).

**What breaks if it fails.** Review capacity planned from the book's tier counts is planned
for a High tier that new accounts will rarely enter. And because the cutoffs are re-taken on
every retrain, a retrain on a riskier book would move them up and hold the workload, not the
risk: the monitoring plan watches the cutoffs themselves as well as the mix
([7.8](monitoring.qmd)).

## The trigger thresholds are meaningful on this data {#ews-trigger-thresholds-are-generic}

**The assumption.** Each threshold in `shared.config.EWS_TRIGGERS` is a policy value a
monitoring officer would recognise — utilisation near the limit, a material rise, a
delinquency of a month or more, a large fall in deposits, repeated overdrafts — and the
assumption is that each is on the scale of the feature it is applied to.

**The evidence.** The largest value each feature takes over the {{< var ews.n_book >}} booked
accounts, against its threshold ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-trigger-performance)):

| Clause | Threshold | Largest value over the book | Accounts it fires on by itself |
|---|---|---|---|
| `util_recent >` | {{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.clause.util_recent.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.clause.util_recent.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.clause.util_recent.n_alone >}} |
| `util_drift >` | {{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.clause.util_drift.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.clause.util_drift.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.clause.util_drift.n_alone >}} |
| `dpd_max >=` | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_max.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_max.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_max.n_alone >}} |
| `dpd_recent >` | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_recent.threshold >}} (hard-coded) | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_recent.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_recent.n_alone >}} |
| `deposit_decline_pct >` | {{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.clause.deposit_decline_pct.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.clause.deposit_decline_pct.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.clause.deposit_decline_pct.n_alone >}} |
| `overdraft_recent >=` | {{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.clause.overdraft_recent.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.clause.overdraft_recent.feature_max >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.clause.overdraft_recent.n_alone >}} |

Days past due in this data are small counts: the generator draws each month's figure from a
Poisson distribution whose mean scales with the true PD, so the worst month on the whole
book is far below the configured delinquency threshold. That clause can never fire, and the
hard-coded "any days past due in the last quarter" clause beside it fires on about half the
book. At the other end, the deposit-decline threshold sits close to the largest decline in
the data, so that trigger fires on very few accounts.

The assumption **holds in part**: four configured thresholds can fire, deposit decline only
rarely; one is unreachable; and the clause doing the delinquency trigger's work is not in the
configuration —
finding 6 ([7.7](limitations.qmd)). Whether the live thresholds pick out accounts that
deteriorate more often than the rest is a question of performance, not scale: finding 7.

**What breaks if it fails.** A threshold on the wrong scale is a control that appears in the
configuration, in the workbench's trigger panel and in this chapter, and does nothing — or
does something no one configured. A reviewer reading `EWS_TRIGGERS` would believe delinquency
is flagged at a month past due; on this data it is flagged at a day.

## The score is a valid input {#ews-the-score-is-a-valid-input}

**The assumption.** `business_score` and `pd_score` come from the saved scorecard
([7.2](data.qmd#ews-score-input)), and the model relies on them being what D4 documents: a
valid ranking of credit risk, computed without leakage.

**The evidence.** Three parts:

- **Computed from the saved model, never from the generator's truth.** `compute_ews_features`
  calls `predict_score_pd` ([7.2](data.qmd#ews-score-input)).
- **In-sample for the scorecard on most accounts.** The scorecard was fitted on applicants
  outside its own held-out share, drawn without regard to booking. The scorecard is a binned
  additive model fitted on a different label, so the optimism this can lend is small, but it
  has not been measured.
- **The score is most of what the model knows.** Ranked by `pd_score` alone, the held-out
  accounts come out about as well as the model ranks them
  ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-benchmark)). D4's findings — a weaker ranking on the booked
  (D4 finding 2), band B under-predicting on the booked (D4 finding 6) — reach this model
  through the score.

The assumption **holds**, with the dependency stated: Early Warning is only as valid as D4,
and on AUC it is not yet shown to be more than D4 (finding 4).

**What breaks if it fails.** A scorecard change is an Early Warning change: retrain,
recalibrate the tier cutoffs and re-assert the gate
([D3](../d3-dependencies.qmd#what-a-scorecard-change-forces)).

## The generator as ground truth

**The assumption.** As in D4 (D4.4): every label in the data was drawn by
`shared/data_generator.py`, and every claim in this chapter is a statement about that
generator, not about a real book ([D1](../d1-purpose.qmd#scope-synthetic-data-real-methods)).

**The evidence.** The generator is code, which is how this chapter can state the ceiling on
ranking ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-ceiling)), say that one trigger clause can never fire, and
say that the label is contemporaneous with its features.

**What breaks if it fails.** On real data the label would come from a real future, the
panel would have gaps and missing months, and the triggers' thresholds would meet
distributions no one has yet looked at. Each of the three is named above or in
[7.7](limitations.qmd) as a question to answer before any real use.
